title: Quicksort 1 - Partition
directAnswer: Pick the first element as the pivot p. Walk the rest of the array once, sending every element smaller than p into a `left` list and every element larger than p into a `right` list. Output `left + [p] + right`. This is one partition step — not a full sort. O(n) time, O(n) extra space with the two helper arrays.

remember.pattern: Single partition around a pivot using two helper arrays
remember.formula:
p = arr[0]
left  = [x for x in arr[1:] if x < p]
right = [x for x in arr[1:] if x > p]
return left + [p] + right
rules: The pivot is the **first** element, `arr[0]`, in this challenge — not the last and not the median.
You are NOT sorting. `left` and `right` only need to be on the correct side of `p`; their internal order is irrelevant.
Output is exactly `left + [p] + right` — one pivot in the middle, smaller on the left, larger on the right.
With the 'one extra array' (out-of-place) version, relative order within each side is preserved; the in-place Hoare/Lomuto version need not preserve it.
Every element except the pivot lands in exactly one side — never lose or duplicate `p`.
whenToUse: You need the building block of quicksort / quickselect
You must place a pivot in its correct relative region without fully sorting
Partitioning a stream into below/above a threshold
Teaching or demonstrating the partition invariant
antiSignals: You need the fully sorted array → that is Quicksort 2 (recurse on both sides)
You need the k-th smallest element → recurse into one side only (quickselect)
Strict O(1) extra space is required → use in-place Lomuto/Hoare partition instead of helper arrays
remember.takeaway: Partition is the heart of quicksort: it places elements relative to a pivot in one linear pass. Master this single step and quicksort, quickselect, and Dutch-flag all fall out of it.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you understand that a partition only guarantees 'pivot in the middle, smaller left, larger right' — not a sorted result — and can implement it cleanly with a chosen pivot.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying to sort the two sides, or accidentally dropping/duplicating the pivot, or putting the pivot itself into a side list.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the partition invariant explicitly, note this out-of-place version is stable while in-place partitions are not, and connect it to quicksort and quickselect.

problemStatement:
Given an array `arr`, partition it around the first element `p = arr[0]` (the pivot).

Reorder the array so that all elements less than `p` come before `p`, and all elements greater than `p` come after it. You do not need to sort the array — just produce a valid partition.

Return the partitioned array.
constraints: All elements are distinct (so no element equals the pivot besides the pivot itself)
understanding: A partition step takes a pivot and arranges the array into three regions: things smaller than the pivot, the pivot itself, and things larger. The sides do not need to be internally sorted. Here the pivot is fixed as the first element, and elements are guaranteed distinct so there is no 'equal to pivot' case to worry about.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Which element is the pivot?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The first element, arr[0]. The challenge fixes it; in real quicksort you'd often randomise.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do the left and right sides need to be sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Only their side relative to the pivot matters — this is a single partition, not a sort.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can there be elements equal to the pivot?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Not in this challenge — elements are distinct. In general you'd pick a consistent side (or do three-way) for equals.

clarifyingQuestions.question: In-place or extra array?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: This variant allows one extra array, so the simplest correct answer builds left/right lists. The in-place version saves space but loses stability.

examples.explanation: Pivot p = 5. Smaller than 5: [4, 3, 2]; larger: [7, 8, 6]. Result is [4,3,2] + [5] + [7,8,6]. Sides keep their original relative order (out-of-place).

diagrams.title: Partition vs full sort
diagrams.caption: Quicksort 1 is one partition; recursing on both sides is Quicksort 2.

approaches.name: Two Helper Arrays (Out-of-Place Partition)
approaches.whenToMention: The clearest correct answer for this challenge — state it directly, it's the intended solution.
hints: The pivot is arr[0]. Every other element is either smaller or larger than it. Where should each go?
Create two empty lists: left for elements < p, right for elements > p. Scan arr[1..] once and route each element.
Concatenate left + [p] + right. Don't sort the sides — a partition only needs them on the correct side of p.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One linear scan over n−1 elements to route them, plus building the result list of size n: O(n) time. The two helper lists hold up to n−1 elements: O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Fix `p = arr[0]`. Walk `arr[1..]` exactly once. Each element is either less than `p` (push to `left`) or greater than `p` (push to `right`) — distinctness guarantees there's no third case. Finally return `left + [p] + right`.

**Why we don't sort the sides.** The deliverable is a *partition*, defined by a single invariant: everything before `p` is smaller and everything after is larger. The internal order of each side carries no meaning for this step. Sorting them would be wasted work (and would actually be the next challenge, Quicksort 2, which recurses).

**Why this out-of-place version is stable.** Because we append elements in the order we encounter them, two elements on the same side keep their original relative order. The in-place partition (swapping within the array) is faster on space but scrambles that order — a distinction worth naming to an interviewer.

**Why the pivot is appended exactly once.** We start the scan at index 1, never re-add `arr[0]` to a side, and place it precisely once in the middle. Losing or duplicating the pivot is the classic partition bug.
approaches.insight: Partition is the irreducible atom of quicksort: 'pivot to its region in O(n)'. Recurse on both sides and you get a sort; recurse on one side and you get O(n)-average selection (quickselect). One routine, three famous algorithms.

dryRun.intro: Pivot p = 5. Route each later element to left (<5) or right (>5), preserving encounter order.

code.python:
def partition(arr: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    p = arr[0]
    left = [x for x in arr[1:] if x < p]
    right = [x for x in arr[1:] if x > p]
    return left + [p] + right

java.explanation: Pivot is the first element, fixed by the challenge.
Start at index 1 so the pivot itself is never routed into a side.
Elements are distinct, so 'not less than' means strictly greater — only two buckets.
Place the pivot exactly once between the two sides.

python.line: left = [x for x in arr[1:] if x < p]
python.explanation: arr[1:] skips the pivot; collect everything smaller, preserving order.
The partition invariant made literal: smaller, pivot, larger.

diagrams.title: Routing elements around the pivot
diagrams.caption: Pivot 5 stays put; each element joins the correct side.

pitfalls: Sorting the left/right sides — that is a full sort, not a partition.
Starting the scan at index 0 and routing the pivot into a side.
Using `<=` for the right side too, duplicating the pivot or mishandling equals (here elements are distinct, but the habit bites later).

edgeCases.behavior: Single element is already partitioned — left and right empty, output [3].

approaches.name: In-Place Lomuto Partition (Space-Optimised)
approaches.whenToMention: Bring up when the interviewer constrains extra space to O(1) or asks how real quicksort avoids allocating arrays.
hints: Can you achieve the same partition without allocating two new arrays?
Keep a boundary index i marking the end of the 'smaller-than-pivot' region. Scan with j; when arr[j] < pivot, swap it into the boundary and advance i.
At the end, swap the pivot into position i so it sits exactly between the two regions.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Single pass with j; each comparison is O(1) and there are n−1 of them. Swaps are in-place, so only O(1) auxiliary space beyond the input array.
approaches.explanation:
The Lomuto scheme partitions in place. With the pivot at index 0, keep a boundary `i` (initialised so the smaller region is empty) and scan `j` from `1` to `n−1`. Whenever `arr[j] < pivot`, advance the boundary and swap `arr[j]` into it. After the scan, swap the pivot into the boundary slot so it lands between the two regions.

**Why this trades stability for space.** Swapping distant elements reorders equal-side elements relative to each other, so the in-place version is *not stable* — but it uses only `O(1)` extra memory, which is why production quicksort uses it.

**Why the result can differ from the out-of-place version.** Both satisfy the partition invariant (smaller | pivot | larger), but the exact arrangement of each side may differ. For HackerRank's checker, any valid partition with the pivot correctly placed is accepted — but if the grader expects the specific `left + [p] + right` order, prefer the helper-array version. Mention this so you pick the version that matches the spec.
approaches.insight: Lomuto's boundary index is a running invariant: everything left of `i` is `< pivot`, everything between `i` and `j` is `≥ pivot`. Maintaining a single boundary pointer in one pass is the same trick behind Move Zeroes and Remove Element.

dryRun.intro: Pivot 4 at index 0. i is the boundary of the <pivot region (starts at 0); swap pivot in at the end.

java.explanation: Boundary of the <pivot region; pivot sits at index 0 so the region starts empty.
Only smaller elements get swapped toward the front.

java.line: int tmp = arr[0]; arr[0] = arr[i]; arr[i] = tmp;
java.explanation: Final swap drops the pivot between the two regions.

python.explanation: Boundary index; everything ≤ i (after the pivot) will be < pivot.
Swap the smaller element into the boundary — in place, no extra array.
Place the pivot at index i, its final partitioned position.

diagrams.title: Lomuto boundary advancing
diagrams.caption: i tracks the end of the <pivot region; the pivot is swapped in last.

pitfalls: Off-by-one on the boundary index i (incrementing before vs after the swap).
Forgetting the final pivot swap — leaves the pivot stranded at index 0.
Assuming stable output — in-place Lomuto reorders the sides, which may mismatch a strict checker.

edgeCases.behavior: Loop body never runs; final swap is a no-op → [3].
j=1: 1<2 → i=1, swap arr[1] with itself; final pivot swap of arr[0],arr[1] → [1,2]. Valid partition (1 < 2).

commonMistakes: Sorting the two sides instead of leaving them merely partitioned.
Dropping or duplicating the pivot when concatenating.
Routing the pivot itself into a side by scanning from index 0.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Sorting the partition sides
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Quicksort 1 asks only for a single partition. Sorting each side does extra work and is actually the next problem (Quicksort 2).
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
left = sorted(x for x in arr[1:] if x < p)
right = sorted(x for x in arr[1:] if x > p)
return left + [p] + right
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
left = [x for x in arr[1:] if x < p]
right = [x for x in arr[1:] if x > p]
return left + [p] + right

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Including the pivot in a side
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Scanning from index 0 (or using <= / >=) puts the pivot into left or right and then again in the middle, duplicating it.

followupVariations.title: Quicksort 2 - Sorting
followupVariations.hint: Recurse this partition on both sides to fully sort the array.

followupVariations.title: Quickselect / Kth Largest Element
followupVariations.hint: Partition, then recurse into only the side containing rank k — O(n) average.

followupVariations.title: Sort Colors (Dutch National Flag)
followupVariations.hint: A three-way partition (<, =, >) handling duplicates of the pivot value.

patternNote: Partition. The O(n) core of quicksort and quickselect: place a pivot into its region with smaller elements before and larger after. Out-of-place is stable and clear; in-place Lomuto is O(1) space but unstable.
